section_summary: This section begins with pages from The Mainichi covering Japan’s April 1946 general election, party speeches, results, alleged violations, food shortages, epidemics, and other domestic news. The diplomatic records then report Soviet and Japanese Communist criticism of the election, intelligence on former Japanese officials in China, and a detailed U.S. counterintelligence review of Tokyo election procedures. The final documents analyze the organization, leadership, purge-related changes, and policies of Japan’s Liberal and Progressive parties during the first postwar months.

subfiles.title: The Mainichi newspaper clipping: election aftermath, returns, and domestic news
subfiles.about: A newspaper section reports on the April 1946 election and a wide range of immediate postwar political and social developments.
subfiles.summary: The clipping contains interviews and party speeches, election results by prefecture, claims of bribery and other violations, and discussion of the unprecedented election of women to the Diet. It also reports Tokyo’s precarious rice supply, typhus and cholera controls, labor and production disputes, and Prince Nashimoto’s release. Advertisements, school notices, employment announcements, film promotions, and commercial notices occupy substantial portions of the pages.

subfiles.title: Circular telegram on Red Star criticism of the Japanese election
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State; James F. Byrnes
subfiles.to: Certain American diplomatic and consular officers
subfiles.about: The telegram summarizes a Red Star article alleging that reactionaries won Japan’s election with Shidehara government and U.S. occupation support.
subfiles.summary: Circular telegram: Red Star calls the election a victory for reactionary forces under Shidehara and occupation patronage, so not representative as the Potsdam Declaration requires.

subfiles.title: Office memorandum concerning distribution of attached China intelligence
subfiles.about: A handwritten note asks whether attached information should be forwarded to the Supreme Commander or the Political Adviser.
subfiles.summary: Office memorandum on sending attached China intelligence about Japan to the Supreme Commander, possibly via the Political Adviser.

subfiles.title: Views of Former Japanese Officials in China Regarding the Future of Japan
subfiles.from: Jason Paige Jr., Strategic Services Unit
subfiles.to: Jack D. Neal, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum describes two opposed currents among former Japanese officials and military personnel in China.
subfiles.summary: Former Japanese officials in China: one group favors collaboration with the US and rebuilding Japan against Soviet expansion; an underground ultranationalist group promotes pan-Asianism and unrest.

subfiles.title: Draft transmittal of memorandum on former Japanese officials in China
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Shanghai
subfiles.about: The draft forwards the Strategic Services Unit memorandum on Japanese officials in China to the Shanghai consulate.
subfiles.summary: Draft transmittal of a Strategic Services Unit report on former Japanese officials in China, noting two major trends among them.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram summarizing Soviet press reports on Japan
subfiles.about: The telegram relays Soviet press reports attacking Japanese agrarian policy, the election result, and alleged secret officer organizations.
subfiles.summary: Soviet press reports Communist opposition to Shidehara's agrarian reform, criticism of MacArthur, and claims that conservatives and suspected war criminals remain influential and that ex-officers are organizing secretly.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 418: Japanese Election Practices Observed in Tokyo
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a counterintelligence assessment of voting and ballot-counting practices in Tokyo during the April election.
subfiles.summary: Investigators considered the election generally honest and fair but identified serious procedural weaknesses capable of producing fraud or error. Outdated voter lists excluded many displaced residents, postcard notices discouraged otherwise eligible voters, precinct records were marked in pencil, and ballot boxes and totals were inadequately reconciled. The report recommends updated registration, secure marking and accounting procedures, printed candidate lists, precinct-level tabulation, clearer invalid-ballot rules, and primary elections to reduce unwieldy candidate fields.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 423: Protest Against Japanese General Election of April 10, 1946 by Japan Communist Party
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards the Japanese Communist Party’s demand that the April election be held again.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson judges the Communist protest of the April 10, 1946 election, citing voter-list defects, intimidation and unscreened militarist candidates, as Moscow-directed. It asks for a new election.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram on Pravda’s appraisal of Japanese politics
subfiles.about: The telegram summarizes a Pravda review blaming occupation policy for conservative dominance in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pravda says the election preserved the power of parties behind Japanese imperialism, and accuses occupation authorities of backing the Liberal Party and obstructing democratic parties.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 490: Forwarding Report on Liberal Party in Japan
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a Government Section report on the origins, leadership, organization, and policies of Japan’s Liberal Party.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the Liberal Party from wartime discussions through Hatoyama Ichirō’s capture of its organization and describes its links to former Seiyūkai politicians, business interests, bureaucrats, and court circles. It reviews the purge of Hatoyama and other leaders, Kōno Ichirō’s subsequent control, Yoshida Shigeru’s selection as prime minister, coalition negotiations, and continuing disputes between professional politicians and bureaucratic appointees. The report portrays the party as highly centralized and weakly responsive to its members, then outlines its program on constitutional government, economic recovery, inflation, agriculture, labor, social insurance, and women’s rights.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for Tokyo Despatch No. 491
subfiles.to: Japanese Affairs and other departmental offices
subfiles.about: The sheet records internal distribution of the forthcoming Tokyo despatch on the Progressive Party.
subfiles.summary: Routing slip assigning copies of Tokyo Despatch No. 491 to Japanese Affairs, Far Eastern offices, Army and Navy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 491: Forwarding Report on Progressive Party in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with partial political intelligence report
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards the opening portion of a Government Section report on Japan’s Progressive Party.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the Progressive Party as a merger of former Minseitō and Seiyūkai professional politicians organized by Shimada Toshio and Machida Chūji through prominent intermediaries. It surveys the principal factions and their competing presidential candidates, including Ugaki Kazushige, Shibusawa Keizō, Konoe Fumimaro, and ultimately Machida. The surviving portion emphasizes factional rivalry, wartime political affiliations, business backing, and the younger group led by Tsurumi Yūsuke; the report continues beyond page 257.
